en: The Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Mahāsāṃghikas. Homage to the Blessed One, who is free from passion!

The wise one, the Buddha— praised by the lords of men and the lords of gods, possessing vast renown throughout the three worlds, the protector who wanders among the worlds— has proclaimed this Prātimokṣa.
Having heard that Prātimokṣa spoken by the Sugata, which is liberation from the suffering of existence, the wise—
by being restrained through the restraint of the six sense faculties— bring an end to birth and death.
Having obtained the three jewels after a long time— Buddha, Dharma, and the pure Sangha—
abandoning the fault of immoral conduct, remain heedful and possess pure morality.
One endowed with virtue, a śramaṇa, crosses over; one endowed with virtue, a brāhmaṇa, crosses over.
One endowed with virtue is honored by men and gods; for the Prātimokṣa belongs to one who is endowed with virtue.
The pure ethical discipline approved by many Buddhas is my foundation, as firm as the earth;
I shall uphold it in the midst of the Saṅgha for the benefit of the world, including its gods.
Introduction:
Of what use is life to those for whom here the nets of unwholesome roots cover the heart, just as lofty clouds obscure the sky?
And for those whose networks of unwholesome roots here quickly go to destruction, like darkness struck down by the sun, their life is truly long-lived.
Of what use is the poṣadha for those whose conduct and observance of precepts are faulty,
who are trapped within the cage of old age and death, and are devoured by the thought of immortality?
And the observance of the *poṣadha* is required for those whose conduct and discipline are blameless—
those who bring an end to old age and death, and who are steadfast in crushing the abode of Māra.
Of what use is the Poṣadha for those who have not attained the stainless [state], whose conduct and morality are broken,
who delight in wrong livelihood, and who speak as if they were immortal?
And the Poṣadha ceremony should be performed for those who are modest, whose conduct and morality have been broken,
yet who delight in right livelihood and possess morality purified by high resolve.
What is the use of the Poṣadha for those who are of immoral conduct,
who have been cast out from the Teacher’s dispensation like a corpse thrown up from the sea?
And the task for them by means of the poṣadha is that which has been prescribed here for those within the three realms;
it is like space for those whose hands are pure and whose minds are liberated.
What is the use of the Poṣadha for those whose six sense-faculties are never guarded,
who have fallen into the domain of Māra, and who avoid the proper range of conduct?
And the task for them is the observance of the *poṣadha*, for those whose six sense-faculties are always well-guarded—
those who are liberated, devoted to the Teacher’s word, the word of the Victor, and the instruction.
What is the use of the Poṣadha for those who themselves claim to possess self-restraint,
yet are of bad character— both toward their fellow practitioners of the holy life and toward the Teacher, as well as gods and humans?
And their task is fulfilled by the Poṣadha ceremony, for in their morality there is nothing to be censured;
indeed, they are free from reproach in every respect among the wise in this world with its gods.
What is the use of the Poṣadha for those who have brought the Teacher’s instruction to ruin— those who have indulged in the five failures and committed the five offenses?

And the task of those who are disciplined in the teaching of the One of Ten Powers— the Fully Awakened One, the All-Seeing— is fulfilled by the poṣadha, for they have cultivated the steps of loving-kindness.
And those in whose hearts dwell the Teacher, the Dharma, and the supreme Assembly;
the training, the recitation, the communal life, contentment, and the word of the Teacher.
For those who have today renounced these things, their poṣadha is fulfilled;
for those who serve the King of Dharma, there exists unconditioned knowledge.
The hand of one who is pure is always pure; for one who is pure and whose actions are clean, the Poṣadha is always [attained].
This applies to you, O Saṃgha, who are always pure.
As long as that [Prātimokṣa] exists within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra in the midst of the community, for that long will the True Dharma and the harmony of the supreme assembly endure.
As long as there are those who teach and those who practice the jewel of the Dharma,
so long shall the True Dharma endure for the benefit of the entire world.
Therefore, being united, harmonious, and full of reverence, attend upon one another and attain the King of Dharma.
The state of nirvāṇa is the absence of decay, self-control, and sorrow.

The monks who have transgressed the boundary are well-prepared, pure, and skilled; they have entered within, are seated, and are of good conduct. They have been counted by means of voting sticks (*śalākā*), and the number of persons is as follows: [the number] of *bhikṣuṇīs* has not yet arrived. Venerable sirs, announce the consent (*chanda*) and the purity (*pāriśuddhi*) of those monks who have not yet arrived. And having announced it, report back: "Which monk is the conveyor of the consent for the *bhikṣuṇīs*? There is no one here who is unordained (*anupasaṃpanna*), no one afflicted with fever (*uṣṇiyukta*), no matricide, and no patricide."
There is no killer of an Arhat; there is no schismatic of the Saṅgha; there is no one who, with a malicious mind, draws blood from a Tathāgata.
There is no nun who is a corrupter; there is no one living in communion through theft;
there is no one living in a separate communion; and there is no one who is not in communion.
There is no one who can surpass him in bodily conduct, nor is there anyone who can equal him in his own self-restraint;
thus do you reflect upon the Blessed One’s disciples, who are eternally pure and whose moral discipline is completely purified.
"Venerable Saṅgha, please listen to me: today for the Saṅgha it is either the fourteenth-day [observance], or the junction-observance (sandhipoṣadha), or the observance of a pure lunar mansion.
So much of the night has passed;
this much remains."
What is the prior duty of the Saṅgha? The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has few duties.
Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me: today is the fifteenth-day Poṣadha of the Saṅgha, under the constellation of Viśuddhi. If...

The Saṃgha has reached the proper time; let the Saṃgha, within this area of ground as much as has been demarcated by the community of monks— extending for a full fathom all around— perform the fortnightly Poṣadha ceremony and recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, until the three exhortations have been announced.

"Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha will perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day and recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* within this area of ground, as far as the community of monks has occupied it, for a distance of one fathom all around.
It is agreeable to the Saṅgha; since there is silence, I shall hold it to be so."
Old age and death face us directly; life is exhausted while what is dear continues; the True Dharma sets;
the torch of the Dharma is extinguished by its teachers;
and those who practice it become few.
Moments, instants, hours, nights, days, months, half-months, seasons, and years pass away;
life is as fleeting and unstable as the water of a mountain stream.
The conditioned formations do not remain still even for the duration of a single uprooting.
Venerable ones, you must accomplish [your goal] through heedfulness.
Why is that?
For the state of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas is attained through heedfulness.
And we say that through heedfulness one attains the unsurpassed and the destruction of acquisitions (*upadhi*).
Therefore, venerable ones, you must accomplish [the goal] by means of that heedfulness;
for Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones perceive ten future benefits.
They prescribe for the disciples the training in higher morality and the points of training;
they also recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. What are these ten?
Namely: for the gathering of the Saṅgha, for the well-being of the Saṅgha,
for the restraint of individuals who are wicked and troublesome, and for the comfortable dwelling of the well-behaved monks.
It is for the purpose of inspiring confidence in those who lack it,
for the increase of those who have confidence, for the destruction of the taints pertaining to the present life, and for the non-occurrence of the taints pertaining to future lives;
so that this teaching may be well-guarded, protected, expanded, and fully elucidated as far as the realms of gods and humans.
Perceiving these ten grounds for censure, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas prescribe the training rules regarding higher morality for their disciples and recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Venerable ones, I shall recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. Listen to it; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.
Should any of you have an offense, let him disclose it.
If there is no offense, you should remain silent.
By your silence,
O Venerable Ones, I shall know that you are pure, just as each individual monk who has been questioned individually gives his response.
In this very same way, when he has been formally admonished up to three times regarding such a matter concerning monks,
if a monk, being thus admonished up to three times, remembers an existing offense and does not disclose it,
there is an intentional falsehood on his part.
Furthermore, venerable ones, intentional lying has been declared by the Blessed One to be an obstructive factor.
Therefore, a monk who remembers [an offense], having fallen into it and seeking purification, should disclose whatever offense he has committed.
Having disclosed it, I find ease; not having disclosed it, I do not. This is the introduction.
Furthermore, venerable ones, these four *pārājika* rules come up for recitation every half-month in the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra.

*PrMoSū(Mā)_Pār.1*: Should any monk, having entered into a formal agreement on training with another monk, without renouncing the training and without disclosing his weakness, engage in sexual intercourse—the act of a layman—even with an animal; ... [the rest of the rule follows] ... he is defeated and no longer in communion.
Together with this, the monk becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; he is not to live in communion and does not obtain communal living with the monks.

This training rule was prescribed by the Blessed One at Vaiśālī when he had been perfectly enlightened for five years, on the twelfth day of the fifth fortnight of winter, while seated facing north in a shadow measuring one and a half *pauruṣas*.

Beginning with the Venerable Yaśika Kalandakaputra, the laying down of this training rule is the Dharma; and that which consists in following it as it has been prescribed—this is called the *anudharma*. (PrMoSū(Mā) Pār.2) Furthermore, whichever monk, from a village or from a forest, should take what is not given, belonging to another, with the intent of theft—

If a monk should take what is not given in such a manner that, were he caught by the owners, they would seize him, kill him, beat him, or banish him, saying, "O man, you are a thief! You are a fool! You are a deluded robber!"—then a monk who takes what is not given in such a manner becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; he is no longer in communion and is not permitted to live together with the monks.

This training rule was prescribed by the Blessed One at Rājagṛha, six years after his full enlightenment, during the winter season, on the second day of the fortnight, in the ninth [watch], while sitting facing east after his midday meal, when the shadow was one and a half *pauruṣas* long.
It was established concerning the venerable Dhanika, who was of the potter caste, as well as King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra and the monk Pāṃsukulika.
The formal establishment of this training rule is the Dharma, and its conformity to what has been thus intended is called the *anudharma*.

PrMoSū(Mā)_Pār.3. Furthermore, if a monk should with his own hand deprive a human being of life, or seek out a weapon for him, or incite him to death, or praise death to him, saying: "O man, what use have you for this wretched, miserable life? Death is better for you than life," [with such] a corrupt mind—[this is a pārājika].
If, by various means, one should incite another to death and praise the beauty of death to them,

and that person should die by that very means and not by any other, this monk also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; he is no longer in communion and is not permitted to live together with the monks.
This training rule concerning Vesālī was prescribed by the Blessed One six years after his full enlightenment, during the winter season,
in the third fortnight, on the tenth day, after the midday meal, while seated facing eastward when the shadow was one and a half *pauruṣas* long,
with reference to many monks who were attendants of the sick and to the wandering ascetic Mṛgadaṇḍika.

The prescription of the training rules is the Dharma; and that which is the conformity to what has been so prescribed is called the *anudharma*. PrMoSū(Mā) Pārājika 4: Furthermore, if a monk, without knowing and without fully understanding, should claim for himself a superhuman state (*uttarimanuṣyadharma*)—that is, this monk should falsely claim to have attained a superior and distinguished realization of the noble knowledge and vision of the Dharma, saying, "I know," or "I see."
Then, at a later time, whether being exhorted by others or not being exhorted, having fallen into an offense and seeking purification, he spoke thus:
"Venerable sirs, not knowing, I said that I know."
"I see this too"—this is empty, false prattle, except as a matter of conceit.
This monk also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; he is not to live in communion and does not obtain co-residence with the monks.
This training rule was prescribed by the Blessed One at Śrāvastī, six years after his full enlightenment, during the winter season.

On the fourth day, at the completion of the thirteenth [fortnight], having eaten, while seated facing north in a shadow measuring half a man’s height, he addressed many village-dwelling monks and the monk Abhimānika: "The laying down of this training rule is the Dharma; and that which is conformity to what has been thus prescribed—this is called the *anudharma* (conformity to the Dharma)."
[1] A park; [2] sexual intercourse; [3] taking what is not given; [4] killing a human being; and claiming to possess superhuman qualities (uttarimanuṣyadharma) through such an act.
Venerable ones, the four *pārājika* rules have been recited.
If a monk should commit any one of these offenses, he becomes *pārājika* and is no longer in communion; he does not obtain co-residence with the monks.
As it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before: he is *pārājika*, no longer in communion, and does not obtain co-residence with the monks.
In this regard, venerable sirs, I ask you: Are you pure in this matter?

A second time, venerable sirs, I ask you: Are you pure in this matter? A third time, venerable sirs, I ask you: Are you pure in this matter? Since there is silence, venerable sirs, I consider you to be pure in this matter.
Furthermore, Venerable Ones, these thirteen *saṃghātiśeṣa* rules come up for recitation in the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra every half-month.
PrMoSū(Mā)_SA.1. Intentionally emitting semen, except during a dream, is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.
PrMoSū(Mā)_SA.2. Whatever monk, with a mind overcome by lust, engages in physical contact with a woman, is [guilty of a *saṃghātiśeṣa*].
If he should enter into such [an act] as taking the hand, or taking the braid of hair, or even touching any other part of the body with a desire for sexual pleasure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
PrMoSū(Mā) SA.3: Furthermore, if a monk, with a perverted mind, should address a woman with coarse and wicked words concerning sexual intercourse—such as, "Come, you two..."—it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"You two are young women"—this is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense. PrMoSū(Mā) SA.4: Furthermore, whichever monk, having descended into a state of lustful passion, should speak in praise of his own bodily service in the presence of a woman, saying: "Sister, this is the foremost of services—that which one provides for a virtuous ascetic such as I."
If one should serve and attend upon a virtuous practitioner of the holy life with this practice—namely, that which is connected with sexual intercourse—it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense.
PrMoSū(Mā)_SA.5. Furthermore, whatever monk should act as a go-between, conveying a message from a woman to a man,
or from a man to a woman, whether for the purpose of marriage or a liaison, even if only to a nun, this is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
When a monk is having a hut built for himself, it must be built without using materials belonging to the Saṅgha and intended for his own use.

In this regard, the measurement is twelve *vitastis* of the Sugata’s span in length, and seven *vitastis* in width. Furthermore, monks must be brought along to designate the site; those monks shall then designate the site.

If a monk, for himself and without a request from others, should have a hut built on a site that requires no excavation but has no space for circumambulation, or on a site that requires excavation and lacks space for circumambulation— even if he builds it himself by his own request,
not for the sake of gain, but for his own purpose— he must lead those monks to inspect the site.
If he exceeds the prescribed dimensions or fails to have the site inspected when there is no space for circumambulation, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

PrMoSū(Mā) SA.7. When a monk is having a large dwelling built for himself that has an owner, he must have monks brought along to designate the site. Those monks must designate the site as one that is free from obstacles and has space for walking around; if there are obstacles, or if there is no space for walking around, it is a *mahallaka* (large) [dwelling].

If a monk should cause a dwelling to be built for himself with a patron, but does not have monks brought there to designate the site, and the site is not designated and is not accessible on all sides, it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.

PrMoSū(Mā) SA.8: If a monk, out of malice, being angry, displeased, and ill-tempered toward another monk, should—without basis—charge that pure monk with an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), he commits a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.

If one should accuse [a monk] of an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), thinking, "Perhaps we might cause this monk to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacarya*)," and at a later time, whether he is examined or not examined, that legal case (*adhikaraṇa*) turns out to be baseless; and in the case of a baseless legal issue, unrighteousness (*adharma*) has been adopted.

If a monk, out of malice and being angry and displeased with another monk, [accuses him] of an offense regarding a legal matter that does not pertain to it, [and he later admits], "I spoke thus out of malice," it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.
PrMoSū(Mā) SA.9: Furthermore, if a monk, being malicious, angry, and displeased with another monk, [accuses him] of an offense regarding a legal matter that pertains to something else...
If one should, on account of some mere trifle— a matter consisting of only a small fraction— accuse an unvanquished monk of a *pārājika* offense, thinking,

"Perhaps we might cause this monk to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacarya*)," then at a later time, whether he is investigated or not, that legal case turns out to be something of a different category altogether.
If a monk takes up even a mere semblance of a legal issue belonging to another category, and persists in his fault saying, "I shall not abandon this fault," it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.
PrMoSū(Mā) SA.10: Furthermore, if a monk should strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha, or for a legal issue conducive to schism...

If that monk should persist in taking up and maintaining [such a position], he should be addressed by the monks thus: "Venerable one, do not strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha, nor persist in taking up and maintaining a legal issue conducive to schism. Let the venerable one be reconciled with the Saṃgha; let the Saṃgha be united, harmonious, living in mutual agreement, without dispute, of one purpose, like milk and water mixed, illuminating the Teacher’s instruction, and dwelling in comfort."
And he dwells in comfort.

If that monk, being thus addressed by the monks, should relinquish that matter, that is good. But if he does not relinquish it, that monk is to be formally admonished and exhorted by the monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter. While being thus admonished up to three times...

Whether being exhorted or being formally admonished, if he should relinquish that matter, it is well; but if he does not relinquish it, and persists in adhering to and maintaining that very matter, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Furthermore, that monk has fellow monks who are his companions.

If one, two, three, or many partisans who follow and support [the schismatic] should, being in agreement with him, speak to those monks for the purpose of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, saying: "Venerable ones, do not say anything at all to this monk—
whether it be good or bad."
"This monk speaks according to the Dharma; this monk speaks according to the Vinaya; this monk acts having adopted and embraced our own will and preference.
Whatever is acceptable and pleasing to this monk is also acceptable and pleasing to us. This monk speaks knowing [the truth], not unknowingly.
Those monks should be addressed by the other monks as follows: "Venerable sirs, do not say that. This monk does not speak according to the Dharma."

"This monk is not one who speaks according to the Vinaya; this monk speaks what is contrary to the Dharma and speaks what is contrary to the Vinaya. This monk speaks without knowing, not with knowledge. Venerable sirs, do not approve of a schism in the Saṅgha; venerable sirs, approve only of harmony in the Saṅgha."

"Venerable sirs, come together with the Saṅgha; for when the Saṅgha is united, harmonious, living in concord, without dispute, with a single objective, like milk and water mixed, illuminating the Teacher’s instruction, it dwells in happiness and comfort. And if those monks, being thus addressed by the monks, should relinquish that matter, that is good. But if they do not relinquish it, those monks are to be exhorted by the monks up to the third time."
They should be exhorted for the relinquishing of that matter;

if, being thus assisted or exhorted up to the third time, they relinquish that matter, that is good. But if they do not relinquish it, and instead persist in adopting that very same matter, [the formal act should be performed].
If he stands holding [his robe], it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense.

PrMoSū(Mā) SA.12: Furthermore, if a monk is of a contentious nature, and when being addressed in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya by other monks regarding the training rules included in the recitation, he makes himself unaddressable.
He spoke thus:
"Venerable sirs, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad;
nor shall I ask anything of the venerable sirs."
"Whether it be good or evil, O Venerable Ones, desist from contradicting my words.

If that monk, when being addressed by other monks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya regarding the training in the precepts included in the recitation, makes himself unaddressable, he should be spoken to thus by the monks: "O Venerable One, do not make yourself unaddressable when being addressed by the monks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya regarding the training in the precepts included in the recitation."
"Venerable sir, let the venerable one address himself; the monks will also address the venerable one in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya regarding his training.

The venerable one should also address the monks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya regarding their training. For it was thus established by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, that these members of this Saṅgha are to be addressed and that they are to be restored from their offenses through mutual interaction."

And if that monk, being thus addressed by the monks, should relinquish that matter, that is good; but if he does not relinquish it, that monk is to be formally admonished and exhorted by the monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter.
If, while being admonished up to three times, he should relinquish that matter...
If he does not desist from this, but persists in adopting and maintaining that very same matter, it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.
PrMoSū(Mā) SA. Furthermore, there are certain monks who dwell in dependence upon a village, city, or town;

they are corrupters of families and of evil conduct. Their evil practices are both seen and heard, the families corrupted by them are both seen and heard, and they are indeed known as corrupters of families.
Those monks of evil conduct should be addressed by the other monks as follows:
"Venerable sirs, indeed your evil conduct is both seen and heard, and families have been corrupted by you, which is also both seen and heard.
Furthermore, Venerable sirs, you are corrupters of families and of evil conduct; therefore, depart from this residence, for enough of your dwelling here!"

And when those monks are thus addressed by the other monks, they should say to those monks: "Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha is acting out of favoritism; the Saṅgha is acting out of malice; the Saṅgha is acting out of delusion; the Saṅgha is acting out of fear;
for the Saṅgha deals with such offenses as these."
If [the Saṃgha] ordains some monks and does not ordain others, those monks should be addressed by the other monks as follows:
"Venerable sirs, do not speak thus; it is not that the monks or the Saṃgha act out of favoritism, nor does the Saṃgha act out of malice, nor does the Saṃgha act out of delusion."
The Saṅgha does not act out of fear; nor does the Saṅgha, on account of such offenses,
ordain some monks while not ordaining others.

Indeed, Venerable Ones, the conduct of those who are like chaff is seen and heard; corrupt families are also seen and heard of, as are those who defile families. Furthermore, Venerable Ones, you follow the customs of the village. "Venerable Ones, depart from this residence;
enough of staying here!"—if monks, being thus addressed by other monks, should relinquish that matter, that is good.
If they do not desist, those monks should be exhorted and admonished by the monks up to three times for the sake of desisting from that matter.
If, being exhorted and admonished up to three times, they desist from that matter, that is good; but if they do not desist and persist in adopting that matter—
If he stands holding it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Prātimokṣasūtra (Mālava): Summary Verse (Uddāna) for the Saṃghāvaśeṣa Offenses.

[1] Intentional emission; [2] taking the hand; [3] illuminating; [4] describing sexual service; [5] acting as a go-between; [6–7] two rules concerning small huts and dwellings; [8] by messenger; [9] of the Saṃgha; [10] one who proceeds toward schism and [11] those who follow him; [12] the difficult-to-speak-to; and [13] those who corrupt families.
PrMoSū(Mā)_SA: These have been recited.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, there are thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine that incur offense upon the first transgression and four that incur offense upon the third admonition; whichever of these offenses a monk has committed, for as long as he knowingly conceals it, for that long must that monk undergo a compulsory probation (*parivāsa*).

A monk who has completed his *parivāsa* must undergo *mānatva* for a further six days within the community of monks. When the monk has performed the *mānatva* and acted in accordance with the Dharma, he should be summoned and informed; there, that monk is to be reintegrated (*āvarhitavya*) by a community of monks consisting of a group of twenty.

If the community of monks consists of fewer than twenty—even by a single monk—and they reintegrate that monk, that monk is not reintegrated and those monks are to be censured. This is the proper procedure in this matter.
Venerable sirs, I ask you: Are you pure in this matter? A second time, venerable sirs, I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time, venerable sirs, I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
Since there is silence, the venerable ones are pure in this matter; thus do I understand it.

Furthermore, venerable ones, these two undetermined rules (aniyata-dharma) come up for recitation every half-month in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. PrMoSū(Mā)_Aniy.1: If a monk should sit alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place suitable for sexual intercourse, and a trustworthy female lay follower, having seen him, should charge him with one of three rules—[the *pārājika*, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or the *pāyattika*]—then that monk, being thus charged by that trustworthy female lay follower, shall undergo investigation regarding those three rules. If he admits to the fact, he is to be dealt with according to whichever of the three rules was charged; if he does not admit it, he must be cleared of the charge through a majority vote of the Saṃgha. These are the two undetermined rules.

If a monk, when being questioned regarding a charge of defeat (*pārājika*), a formal meeting offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), or an offense entailing confession (*pāyattika*), admits to it by means of one or another of these three categories of offenses, he should be dealt with according to one or another of those three offenses—
whether it be *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or *pāyattika*— in accordance with whatever his own credible statement may be.

If a female lay follower (*upāsikā*), having seen [the offense], should speak according to the Dharma, then that monk is to be dealt with according to the Dharma; this rule is undetermined (*aniyata*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that the seat is concealed, nor is it fit for use; yet it is indeed sufficient to address a woman with coarse speech. *PrMoSū(Mā)_Aniyata 2*.

If a monk, with a wicked mind intent on sexual intercourse, should sit alone with a woman in secret on a seat such as that, and a female lay follower of trustworthy speech, having seen him, should charge him with one or another of the two kinds of offenses— either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or [another offense]— [then he is to be dealt with accordingly].
If a monk, while acknowledging his sitting [with a woman], is charged with a *pācattika* offense, he should be dealt with according to one of two rules:
either by a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or by a *pācattika*.

Furthermore, whatever reliable testimony a female lay follower (upāsikā), having seen [the matter], may provide according to the Dharma, by that very testimony that monk is to be dealt with according to the Dharma; this rule is also undetermined (aniyata).
A garden [1], a concealed seat [2], and a secluded place for sitting.
The Indeterminate Rules have been recited.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, there are two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharma). Regarding this, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
Since the venerable ones are silent, I consider the venerable ones to be pure in this matter.
Furthermore, venerable ones, these thirty *niḥsargika-pācattika* rules come up for recitation every half-month in the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra.

PrMoSū(Mā) NP.1: When a robe has been finished and the *kaṭhina* period has ended, a monk may keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days. If he should keep it longer than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.

PrMoSū(Mā) NP.2. When a robe has been made by a monk and the kaṭhina period has been suspended, if a monk should live apart from any one of his three robes for even a single night, except by the authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.3. When a monk’s robes have been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, if an out-of-season robe should arise for a monk, that monk, desiring it, may accept it.
Having accepted it, he must have those robes made up as quickly as possible.
While that monk is having the robes made up, if those robes are not completed, the monk may keep that robe for at most one month. After that, he must relinquish it.
If a monk, with the hope of fulfilling a deficiency, should set aside a robe for another, whether such a hope exists or not, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
Furthermore, if a monk should accept a robe from a nun who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.5. If a monk should have a robe washed, dyed, or beaten for another unrelated nun, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.6. If a monk should ask a robe from an unrelated householder or householder’s son, except at the proper time, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
In this regard, this is the proper occasion: when a monk’s robe has been lost.
This is the occasion here.
For a monk whose robe has been lost, it is permissible to ask a householder or a householder’s son who is not a relative for a robe.

If he has been addressed by him and is agreed upon, one should offer many robes; when thus invited, a monk may accept robes with the inner and upper robe as the maximum. If he should accept more than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
Furthermore, with reference to a certain monk, two householders have prepared and intended various means for procuring robes, thinking: "With these means for procuring robes,
having purchased a robe, we shall clothe the monk named so-and-so with a robe."
And in that case, if a monk, not having been previously invited, should go there and make a request, saying: "It would be well, venerable sirs,

if you were to purchase a robe with these robe-funds and provide a robe for the monk named so-and-so," and if both parties together, out of a desire for what is good, should procure a robe in such a manner, then when the robe is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.

Furthermore, if, with reference to a certain monk, two individuals— a householder and a housewife— each separately prepare and provide funds for the purchase of a robe, thinking, "With these respective funds for the purchase of robes,
having each purchased a robe individually, we shall [give them] to the monk named so-and-so," [and if the monk accepts them...]
"We shall each provide a robe.

In this case, if a monk, not having been previously invited, should go there and form a conceptual intention, saying: "It would be well indeed, O venerable one, if you and you, sister, were to purchase individual robes with these respective funds for purchasing robes and [provide] such [a robe]," [he commits an offense].
"Cover each of us with a robe,
either of such a kind or of such a kind, both together.
Out of a desire for something beautiful, when the robe has been completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pācattika* offense.

Furthermore, if a king or one who is like a king, having in mind a certain monk, should send messengers with funds for the purchase of robes, that monk, having approached them, should speak thus to that person:
"Indeed, these funds for the purchase of robes have been sent by such-and-such a king or one like a king, intended for the Venerable One; may the Venerable One accept them."
That monk should speak to that messenger thus: "Venerable sir, it is not permissible for a monk to accept money intended for robes;
however, we do accept a robe that is offered at the proper time and is allowable.
When this has been said, that messenger should inform that monk accordingly.
Furthermore, noble one, there are some who perform services for the monks.
If a monk desires [services], he should not designate his own attendants as service-providers.
Rather, O Venerable One, these monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) perform services for the monks as the monks' service-providers.

Thus addressed, that messenger should go to where the attendants are and say to those very attendants: "It would be well, venerable attendants, if you were to purchase a robe with these robe-funds and clothe such-and-such a monk with that robe."

At the proper time and on a suitable occasion, in a manner that is appropriate and blameless, that messenger, having informed those attendants, should approach the monk and say to him: "The attendants whom the Noble One designated have been informed by me; I shall go to them, and they will provide the robes."

When a monk who requires robes has need of them at the proper time and on the proper occasion for suitable and blameless robes, he should go to those attendants and, having approached them, request and inform those attendants one, two, or three times:
"Venerable sirs, please provide me, the monk, with robes. If, while urging and informing them one, two, or three times, [he obtains them]...
"He should complete that robe-cloth; this is good. If he does not complete it, the monk should stand silently in the designated place for four times, five times, or at most six times.
If, while standing silently in the designated place for four times, five times, or at most six times, he completes that robe-cloth..."
If this [cloth] is not successful, he should be told, "Go quickly or come; have that robe-cloth prepared.
If the robe-cloth is prepared, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissargika-pācattika*).
If it is not prepared, he should go to where those robe-funds were sent by the king or one who serves the king.

In that case, that monk should either go there himself or send a suitable representative with the message: "Venerable sirs, these robe-funds have been sent for the sake of a certain monk named so-and-so; however, they do not serve any purpose for that monk."
"He who yokes [himself] according to his own nature—that wise one shall not fall away from the Dharma. This is the *anusāmīcī*.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) for the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra (Mānuṣya).

[1] Ten days, [2] staying away, [3] at an improper time, [4] receiving, [5] washing, [6] begging, [7–8] the two regarding the long robe and the inner robe, [9] by way of alternative, [10] and the king— this is the first section.
If a monk should have a new rug made of pure white sheep’s wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.12. When a monk is having a new rug made, two parts of pure black sheep’s wool must be taken;
a third part of white wool; and a fourth part of brown wool. Should he take more than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.13. Furthermore, whatever monk should have a new rug made mixed with silk and sheep’s wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.14. When a monk has a new rug made, it must be kept for at least six years.

If, after that, a monk—whether he has disposed of his old rug or not—should have another new rug made out of a desire for what is beautiful, except by means of a formal exchange, it is a *nissargika-pācattika*.

PrMoSū(Mā) NP.15. When a monk is having a new sitting mat made, he must take a portion from all sides of the old sitting mat equal to a Sugata-span for the purpose of disfiguring the new one; if a monk should have a new sitting mat made without taking [this portion], it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
Furthermore, when wool from sheep arises for a monk who has set out on a journey, that monk, if he so desires, may accept it. Having accepted it, he may carry it himself at most three *yojanas*.
If he carries it beyond that, whether or not he places it in another carrier, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.17. Should any monk have wool from sheep washed, dyed, or carded by a nun who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.18. Should any monk with his own hand take up gold or silver, or cause it to be taken up, or say, "Put this here," it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
Or if she should consent to what has been entrusted to her, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.

If a monk should engage in various kinds of buying, selling, or commercial transactions— namely, saying "buy this," "buy from here," "for so much," or "buy for such an amount"— it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
If a monk should engage in various kinds of transactions involving gold, silver, or their manufactured forms, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
Prātimokṣasūtra (Mālava): Summary Verse for the Naiḥsargika Pāyattikas [11–20]:

[11–12] Two rules concerning pure black wool; [13] mixed with *kaiśeya* silk; [14] six years; [15] a sitting mat; [16] on the road; [17] having it unbraided; [18] with one's own hand; [19] buying and selling;
[20] by means of bartering goods.
The second section.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.21. A monk may keep an extra bowl for a maximum of ten days; if he should keep it longer than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.

PrMoSū(Mā) NP.22. Furthermore, if a monk, while possessing a bowl that has less than five mends, should seek another new bowl on account of this [rule], that monk must relinquish that bowl in the assembly of monks.
Whichever bowl is the last among those bowls in the assembly of monks shall be given to him.
It should be given to that monk.

Thus, O Venerable One, that bowl must be used by you until it breaks; [if it is not, there is an offense of] *naiḥsargika-pācattika*. Furthermore, regarding those medicines which are to be consumed by the sick:
Namely: ghee, oil, honey, and molasses. A sick monk is permitted to accept such things even if they have not been formally prepared for him, provided he consumes them as a seven-day store.
Whatever remains must be relinquished; it must be relinquished, and if one should eat or consume more than that, or fail to relinquish what remains, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā) NP.24: Furthermore, if a monk, having given a robe to another monk, becomes angry and displeased due to some offense and, being resentful, [acts as follows...]
If she should tear it herself, or cause it to be torn, or take back the robe-cloth of a nun, or say, "I will not give it to you," it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
When one month of the summer retreat remains, a monk should seek out a rainy-season robe (*varṣāśāṭikā-cīvara*); when half a month remains, he should store it away.

Furthermore, if a monk, having made up his mind during the interval [between the end of the rains retreat and the robe season], should seek out a rain-cloak (*varṣāśāṭikā*) robe and have it woven, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
Moreover, if a monk himself should request thread and have a weaver weave a robe for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.

Furthermore, if a certain householder or householder’s son, having intended for certain monks, should have a weaver weave a robe for them, those monks, not having been previously invited, should not go to him and make a request,
saying: "It would be well, venerable sir, if you would make this robe long, make it wide, and make it well-woven."
Have it well-planed and have it well-scrubbed;
perhaps we might provide you with some small amount,
even a single māsaka coin.
Whether it be half a māsaka, or a bowl of alms-food, or even more than a bowl of alms-food;
and having spoken thus to him, that monk does not provide even such a measure as a single māsaka.
Whether it be half a māṣaka,
or a bowl of alms-food, or even more than a bowl of alms-food;
when the robe has been completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.

PrMoSū(Mā) NP.28. Furthermore, when ten days remain before the three-month period ending on the full moon of Kārttika, if an urgent robe-material should arise for a monk, and he, considering it urgent, should accept it, he must keep it until the time for the distribution of robes.
If he should keep it beyond that, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
Furthermore, it is during the three-month rains retreat, on the full moon day of Kārttika, that monks dwell in forest lodgings at a time that is dangerous, fearful,
and considered insecure.
A monk who so desires must deposit one of his three robes within a village.

If there should arise for that monk some reason for being separated from that robe, he may remain separated from it for at most six days. If he remains separated from it longer than that, except by the authority of the Saṃgha, it is a *nissargika-pācattika*.
If a monk, knowing that a gain belonging to the community has been dedicated to the Saṅgha, should appropriate it for himself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

Prātimokṣasūtra (Mālava): Summary Verse for the Nissaggiya Pācittiyas [21]: The bowl, [22] the binding, [23] medicine, [24] non-interruption, [25] the eight-month rainy-season robe, [26–27] two concerning the weaver, [28] the ten-day limit on what has not arrived, [29] the extra rain-robe, [30] and by means of redirection—this is the third section.

Venerable sirs, the thirty *niḥsargika-pācattika* dharmas have been recited. Regarding this, venerable sirs, I ask: are you pure in this matter? A second time, venerable sirs, I ask: are you pure in this matter?
A third time, venerable ones, I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
Since there is silence, the venerable ones are pure in this; thus do I understand it.
Furthermore, venerable ones, these ninety-two rules of pure *pācattika* come up for recitation every half-month in the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra.
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.1. In the case of intentional lying, there is a *pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.2. In the case of malicious speech, there is a *pācattika*. PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.3. In the case of slander against a monk, there is a *pācattika*.

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.4: Should any monk, knowing that formal acts (karmans) of the Saṃgha have been carried out in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya and have been settled, stir them up again, thinking, "This formal act must be performed once more," and doing so for no other reason than this,
it is a Pācattika offense for that monk to stir up what has been settled.

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 5: Should any monk preach the Dharma to a woman in an improper place, beyond five or six words, except in the presence of a person capable of understanding, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 6: Should any monk recite the Dharma word by word to a person who has not received full ordination, it is an offense of expiation.

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 7: Should any monk, in the presence of a person who has not received full ordination, claim for himself a superhuman state that is pure, noble, and a ground of knowledge—namely, the attainment of the fruit of the holy life—it is an offense of expiation.
If one makes a claim regarding the attainment of two specific [stages], saying "I know" or "I see," on that occasion there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 8: Should any monk, knowing it to be a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-āpatti*), report it to an unordained person, except when there is a formal authorization for disclosure, it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*).
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.
9: Should any monk, having previously given his consent when a gain belonging to the community was being distributed, [later object to it]... [it is an offense of expiation].

If, afterwards, a woman should approach [the monks] with a formal charge, saying, "Venerable sirs, just as you have been introduced to one another, an individual is diverting to another individual a vehicle belonging to the community or a gain dedicated to the Saṅgha," it is a *pācattika* offense.
PrMoSū(Mā)_Pāc.10. Furthermore, if a monk, while the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is being recited every half-month, should say:

"What, venerable ones, is the use of these minor and trivial rules of training being recited, which lead only to remorse, frustration, and distress for the monks? this is an offense of expiation (pācattika) for disparaging the training.
Prātimokṣasūtra (Mālava): Pācittiya Summary Verse:
[1] Falsehood, [2] disregarding, [3] slander, [4] uprooting, [5] teaching the Dharma, [6] word by word, [7] qualification, [8] making known, [9] according to intimacy, [10] by reproaching.
This is the first section.
Pācittiya 11: In destroying a collection of seeds or a collection of living beings, there is an offense of expiation.
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.12. To speak ill of others or to cause them harm is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.13: To recite [the Prātimokṣa] while diminishing [the number of rules] is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

PrMoSū(Mā)_Pāc.14. Should any monk, having knowingly placed or knowingly caused to be placed in a communal monastery for monks— whether in an open space— a bed, a bench, a mattress, a pillow with four corners, a bolster, or a cushion, and then depart without putting it away, or without having it put away, or without taking leave, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

Pācittiya 15: Should any monk, having spread out or caused to be spread out a bed within a communal monastery belonging to the Saṃgha, depart from there without putting it away, or causing it to be put away, or without taking leave, it is a Pācittiya offense.

Pācittiya 16: Should any monk, being malicious, angry, and displeased with another monk, drive him out or cause him to be driven out from a communal monastery belonging to the Saṃgha, or even so much as say, "Get out, monk," it is a Pācittiya offense.

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.17: Should any monk, knowing that in a communal monastery belonging to the monks, beds have already been assigned by the monks, go there later and assign his own bed in the middle, thinking, "Whoever will have to move out will depart"—
if he does this for no other reason than that, it is a *pācattika* offense for the removal of that monk's bedding.
If a monk, having struck with his foot upon a small hut situated in the open air above a communal dwelling for monks, should sit down or lie down upon a bed or a bench,
it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
If a monk, knowing it contains living beings, should sprinkle or cause grass or clay to be sprinkled with water containing living beings, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.20. When a monk is having a large dwelling built, from the door-frames up to the placement of the bolts, including the preparation of the light-shafts, he should authorize two or three layers of roofing.
If he should authorize more than that, even if it is on ground with little vegetation, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

Prātimokṣasūtra (Mālava) Pācittiya Summary Verse [11]: Seed; [12] speaking of another; [13] reviling; [14] bed; [15] couch; [16] storing; [17] one who has arrived first; [18] in the air; [19] water; [20] covering.
The second chapter.

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.21: Should any monk, not being authorized, exhort the nuns, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.22: Even if authorized, should a monk exhort the nuns at an improper time, when the sun has set and the dawn has not yet risen, it is an offense of expiation.

Pācittiya 23: Should any monk, seeking an opportunity for admonition, approach the dwelling place of the nuns without having first informed a monk who is present, except on an appropriate occasion, it is a pācittiya.
In this regard, the occasion is when a sick bhikṣuṇī is to be exhorted and instructed; this is the occasion here.
If a monk should say to another monk, "Venerable one, a monk is instructing a nun for the sake of material gain," it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
If a monk should sit alone with a nun in private on a secluded seat for one day and night, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.26: Should any monk, having made an appointment with a nun, travel along a road together, even as far as another village, except at the proper time, it is a *pācattika*.
Herein, this is the proper time:
when the road is dangerous, fearful, and full of apprehension; this is the proper time in this case.

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.27: Should any monk, having made an appointment with a nun, board the same boat—whether going upstream or downstream—with the exception of crossing over to the other bank, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.28: Should any monk give a robe to a nun who is not a relative, except for a discarded robe, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
If a monk should sew or cause another monk’s robe to be sewn for a nun who is not a relative, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
If a monk, knowing that almsfood has been prepared by a nun, should consume it—except in the case of a prior engagement with a householder—that is a *pācattika*.

[21] A garden; [22] one who is not authorized; [23] even one who is authorized; [24] exhortation; [25] material gain; [26] sitting together; [27] a journey on a road; [28] and a boat; [29] he gives; [30] he sews; by means of ripening.
The third chapter.
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 31. A monk who is not ill may consume food from a lodging-house for at most one day. If he consumes it beyond that, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 32: Eating in succession, except at the proper time, is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Herein, this is the proper time:
the time of illness and the time for the distribution of robes; this is the proper time here.

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 33. Should any monk, having been invited to eat and having risen from his seat, eat or consume solid or soft food that has not been made into "extra" (anatirikta), it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 34. Should any monk, knowing that another monk has already eaten and has risen from his seat after being invited, and looking for an opportunity to cause him to eat, invite him with solid or soft food that has not been made into "extra," saying, "Come, monk, eat what is fit to be eaten"—it is an offense of expiation.
Or if she should say, "Eat," [and he eats], it is a pācattika offense once he has eaten.

Pācittiya 35: Should any bhikṣu eat solid food that has not been given and not formally accepted, by means of the gateway of the mouth—with the exception of water and tooth-sticks—it is a pācittika offense.
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.36. Eating at an improper time is an offense of expiation (pācattika). PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.37. Eating food that has been stored is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.38. Furthermore, if someone approaches a monk on the bank [of a river] and offers him cakes or dough-balls, a monk who has been so invited may accept no more than what fills three bowls.
Then it should be accepted;

having accepted it, it should be brought outside the gate; having brought it outside the gate, it should be eaten and consumed after sharing it with monks who are not ill. If one accepts more than that and brings it outside the gate...
If a monk, having shared or not shared [these foods] with monks who are not ill, should chew or eat them, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

Furthermore, regarding those foods which are considered delicacies—namely, ghee, sesame oil, honey, molasses, milk, curds, fish, and meat—if a monk, having accepted such delicacies... [PrMoSū(Mā)_Pāc.39]... [text continues].

If one who is not ill, having requested food for oneself from a householder on the bank, should eat it or consume it—whether by requesting it oneself or having it requested—there is an offense of expiation (pācittika).

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 40: Eating in a group, except at the proper time, is an offense of expiation. Herein, this is the proper time: the time of illness, the time of the distribution of robes, the time of traveling on a journey, the time of boarding a boat, a great festival, and when a meal is provided by a caravan; these are the proper times here.

[The offenses regarding] a garden [31], a lodging [32], a succession [33], the invitation [34], sitting down [35], what is not given [36], the wrong time [37], storing up [38], barley-meal [39], and the formal announcement [40]— these are [the offenses] through eating in a group.
The fourth section.

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 41. Whatever monk, not being ill, for his own sake, should kindle a fire or cause one to be kindled with grass, wood, cow dung, a piece of brick, chaff, or rubbish—except at the proper time—it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc. 42. Whatever monk should lie down in the same dwelling together with a person who has not received full ordination for more than two or three nights—it is an offense of expiation.

Pācittiya 43: Should any monk, having given his consent for a formal act (karman) of the monks, later—being malicious, resentful, angry, and displeased—should speak thus: "My consent was not given; my consent was wrongly given; these acts were not performed;
these acts were ill-performed; I do not give my consent to those acts," he commits a Pācittiya offense.

PrMoSū(Mā) Pāc.44: Should any monk speak thus to another monk: "Come, venerable one, let us enter the village for alms; I will give you something there," and having given him something there, or not having given him anything, he subsequently reviles him, saying: "Go away, venerable one! It is not comfortable for me to be with you. This is a *pācattika*.
Whether it be for conversation or for sitting together—if, having made this very thing the reason, one incites another monk [to leave], it is a *pācattika* offense.

This applies even when it is comfortable for me alone for conversation or for sitting together; making this the sole reason, there is no other [allowable motive]. It is a *pācattika* offense for the incitement of that monk.

Pācittiya 45: Should any monk speak thus to other monks: "Venerable sirs, as I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, those things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not sufficient to be an obstruction for one who indulges in them," that monk should be addressed by the other monks as follows: "Venerable sir, do not speak thus; do not misrepresent the Blessed One."

If that monk, being devoid of wisdom and lacking discernment, [insists that] these things which are obstacles are indeed "obstructive factors" (*antarāyika-dharma*) as declared by the Blessed One— whereby for one who indulges in them, they are sufficient to constitute an obstacle— and if, when thus addressed by the monks, he does not relinquish that matter, then that monk is to be exhorted and admonished by the monks regarding that matter up to three times.

If, while being exhorted or admonished up to the third time for the sake of relinquishing [the offense], he should relinquish that matter, it is well; but if he does not relinquish it, that monk is to be suspended by the Saṃgha in its entirety. This is the *pācattika* offense for the suspension of that monk.
Pācittiya 46: Should any monk, knowing that another monk has been thus suspended by a unanimous Saṃgha according to the Dharma and the Vinaya—
having acted in accordance with what he said, for not relinquishing an evil view— and yet, while that [suspension] has not been performed in accordance with the Dharma,
should eat together with him, or live together with him, or share a dwelling with him, it is a Pācittiya.

PrMoSū(Mā)_Pāc.47. If a novice (śramaṇudeśa) should speak thus: "Venerable sirs, as I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, those sensual pleasures which have been declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction for one who indulges in them," that novice is to be addressed by the monks in this way: "Do not, venerable novice, speak thus; do not misrepresent the Blessed One."
"Venerable one, those sensual desires which are grasped improperly are indeed obstacles.
The Blessed One has declared that sensual desires are obstacles, and that they are sufficient to create an obstacle for one who indulges in them.
If, when addressed by the monks in this manner, that novice monk should relinquish that matter, that is good."
And if that novice monk should not desist, he is to be exhorted and admonished by the monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter.
If, being exhorted or admonished up to three times, he should relinquish that matter, that is good; but if he does not relinquish it, that novice monk [is to be dealt with accordingly].

"A monk must indeed be expelled. From this day forward, O venerable one, you, a novice, shall no longer designate the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, as your teacher. depart, go away, and flee!"

PrMoSū(Mā)_Pratid.3: Furthermore, when monks are invited to eat in a house and a nun is there—"

Regarding the Dharma and the secondary Dharma (*anudharma*):

furthermore, this Dharma and Vinaya of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One— whether it has entered the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, is included within the Sūtras, or is any other teaching that constitutes the secondary Dharma of the Dharma— is therein [to be practiced].
For when all are complete, united, living in harmony, without dispute, focused on a single goal, blending like milk and water, illuminating the Teacher’s dispensation,
and dwelling in happiness and comfort, there is no need for further instruction regarding the training rules.
Patience is the supreme austerity; the Buddhas declare that endurance is supreme Nirvana.
For one who harms others is not a renunciant, nor is one who oppresses others a true Śramaṇa.

This is the Prātimokṣa in brief, [spoken] by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, not long after his full enlightenment, within a community of monks free from internal strife.
Well-spoken.
Speaking without exaggeration, not harming others, restraint according to the Prātimokṣa,
moderation in food, dwelling in remote lodgings, and application to higher mental training— this is the instruction of the Buddhas.

This is the Prātimokṣa, well-spoken in brief by that Blessed One, the Śaikṣin, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, not long after his full enlightenment, within a community of monks free from blemish:
"Do not be negligent regarding the higher mind; train in the states of the Sage who practices silence.
For the Protector, who is ever mindful and perfectly tranquil, no sorrows arise."
This is the Prātimokṣa, well-spoken in brief by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One Viśvabhū, to the community of monks free from blemish.
The non-doing of all evil, the attainment of the wholesome, and the complete subduing of one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

This is the well-spoken Prātimokṣa, spoken in brief by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One Krukrucchanda, not long after his full awakening, when the community of monks was free from blemish.
Just as a bee, without harming the color or fragrance of a flower, departs taking its nectar, so should a sage conduct himself in a village.
He should not attend to the faults of others, nor to what they have done or left undone.
But one should examine for oneself both what has been done and what has not been done.

This is the well-spoken *Prātimokṣa* in brief, spoken by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Konākamuni, not long after his full enlightenment, when the community of monks was free from blemish.
(PrMoSū(Mā) Conclusion v.7): There is no meditative absorption for one lacking wisdom; there is no wisdom for one who does not practice meditation.
He who possesses both meditative concentration and wisdom is indeed close to Nirvana.
In this regard, this is the beginning:
here, for a wise monk, there is guarding of the sense faculties, restraint according to the rules of conduct, and observance of the Prātimokṣa vows.
One should always associate with the virtuous, who live a pure life and are untiring;
one should be hospitable and skilled in proper conduct.
Then, abounding in joy, the monk is as if in the very presence of nirvana.

This is the Prātimokṣa, well-spoken in brief by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, not long after his full enlightenment, when the community of monks was free from internal strife.
Restraint of the eye is good; restraint of the ear is good;
restraint of the nose is good; restraint of the tongue is good;
restraint of the body is good; restraint of the mind is good.
A monk who is restrained in all respects is liberated from all suffering.

This is the well-spoken Prātimokṣa in brief, delivered by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the sovereign of the Śākyas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha, not long after his full enlightenment, when the community of monks was free from internal strife.
These are the Prātimokṣas of the glorious, perfectly enlightened ones.

These are the seventeen powers.
